answer: The passages were not included, so this answer is based on the standard published descriptions of the two methods. node2vec exploits structure through biased second-order random walks. Its parameters p (return) and q (in-out) control whether each walk step stays near the start node (BFS-like, capturing structural equivalence) or moves outward (DFS-like, capturing community/homophily). The walk sequences are then fed to skip-gram with negative sampling, so structure enters through the sampled contexts. LINE (2nd-order) does not use random walks. It models first-order proximity (direct edge strength) and second-order proximity (similarity of neighborhoods, via shared context nodes), with separate vertex and context embeddings. It optimizes a KL-divergence-based objective by sampling edges directly, weighted by edge weight, with negative sampling. Its exploitation of structure is therefore limited to direct and two-hop neighborhood similarity, while node2vec's walks reach broader multi-hop structure that can be tuned between local and global views. In short, node2vec learns from tunable random-walk co-occurrences, while LINE learns from explicit first- and second-order edge-based proximities.
